questions.question: How do you use the fetch API correctly, including error handling and cancellation?
questions.title: Fetch Api
questions.direct_answer: fetch(url, options) returns a promise resolving to a Response. Key behaviors: fetch only rejects on NETWORK errors — HTTP 404/500 are still successful fetches (check response.ok or response.status); the body is a stream read via response.json()/text() (each readable once); options carry method, headers, body (JSON needs JSON.stringify + Content-Type), and signal for AbortController cancellation.

sections.title: Interview Answer
Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    F[fetch] -->|network fail / CORS / abort| REJ[rejects]
    F -->|any HTTP response| RES[resolves - even 404/500]
    RES --> OK{res.ok?}
    OK -->|yes| BODY[res.json - one-shot stream]
    OK -->|no| ERR[check res.status - throw app error]
    BODY -->|invalid JSON| PARSE[res.json rejects]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
Why fetch doesn't throw on 4xx/5xx (the design reasoning): the Response object represents the COMPLETED network exchange. DNS failure, refused connection, CORS block — those reject because no response exists. A 404 response is a successful HTTP conversation about a missing resource — the fetch succeeded at its job (transport), and the status code is application semantics the caller interprets. This is why res.ok exists: a convenience for the 200–299 range check.

The body-as-stream model (the depth marker): the Response body is a ReadableStream. res.json(), res.text(), res.formData() consume it exactly once — they return promises because the stream arrives asynchronously. To read a body twice (e.g., log the raw text AND parse it), you clone first: `const [a, b] = await Promise.all([res.clone().text(), res.json()])`. This model is what enables fetch to handle huge downloads efficiently — you can process chunks via res.body.getReader() without buffering the whole payload.

The cancellation plumbing (the production pattern): AbortController is the web's standard cancellation token. Beyond fetch, it cancels any operation written to honor a signal — the reason it's the same mechanism React Query and most modern SDKs use. Compose it with race for timeouts (setTimeout(() => ctrl.abort(), 5000)), with useEffect cleanup for component unmounts, and with 'stale request' logic (each new search aborts the previous request — the fix for out-of-order response races).
